title: When is the domination polynomial of a random graph ultra-log-concave?
shortTitle: Random graphs have log-concave domination polynomials
oneLine: Almost all graphs are ultra-log-concave; at the boundary scale p(log n)² bounded, a Poisson count decides.
abstract: A dominating set in a network is a set of nodes such that every node is in the set or linked to one in it. Counting the dominating sets of each size gives the coefficients of the domination polynomial. Cameron checked every graph with at most nine vertices, found exactly one whose counts are not log-concave, and conjectured that almost all graphs have log-concave counts. This candidate proves that in the random graph G(n,p) with p at most 1-ε and p(log n)² tending to infinity, the domination polynomial is ultra-log-concave, hence log-concave, with probability tending to one; at p = 1/2 this covers almost all graphs, labelled or unlabelled, and answers Cameron's question. The scale is the right one for a guarantee valid along every density sequence: when p(log n)² stays bounded, tuned densities make log-concavity fail with an explicit limiting probability, decided by whether the Poisson-like number of smallest dominating sets exceeds a threshold. For p = θ/(log n)² the probability has no limit. A binomial convex-order bound for the size of a weighted random dominating set follows. Small computations agree: at p = 1/2, ultra-log-concavity fails for 636 of the 32,768 labelled graphs on 6 vertices. Limits: asymptotic results with no explicit n; very dense graphs and densities with p(log n)² tending to zero are not covered; the finite computations are illustrations. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

evidence: A 14-page paper with a plain introduction (the question, why it is natural, what was known, what is new, the mechanism and a roadmap) and written proofs of every result. Five Python programs accompany it: verify.py checks the mean formula exactly over all labelled graphs with up to 5 vertices and the upper-range counting inequality on every three-set family with up to 6 points; audit_checks.py recounts all graphs with up to 6 vertices, verifies 1904 instances of the hypergeometric identity exactly and checks threshold rounding at very large n; check_tuning.py evaluates the tuned densities of Theorem 2.3; finite_n.py tabulates failures for graphs with up to 18 vertices (exhaustive up to 6, then 20,000 seeded samples per size); natural_density.py illustrates the slow convergence for p = 1/(log n)². A clean replay reproduced every recorded output byte for byte in Python's optimised mode; making the tail bound too strong or the tuning tolerance negative makes the scripts fail; Linux CI reruns all five under a declared comparison policy. The computations accompany the written proofs; they do not replace them.

keyResults: Theorem 2.1 (proof): in G(n,p) with p ≤ 1-ε and p(log n)² → ∞, with high probability the domination polynomial is ultra-log-concave (hence log-concave), strictly exactly for γ ≤ k ≤ n-δ.
Corollary 2.2 (proof): almost all graphs, labelled or counted up to isomorphism, have an ultra-log-concave domination polynomial; this answers Cameron's question.

Theorem 2.3 (proof): when p(log n)² → θ, tuned densities give P(log-concave) and P(ultra-log-concave) tending to explicit Poisson probabilities, such as P{Pois(λ) < λe^θ}; at θ = 0 and λ = log 2 the limit is 1/2.
Theorem 2.5 (proof): for p = θ/(log n)², P(ultra-log-concave) → 1 along a set of n of natural density one, but its lim inf is at most exp(-e^(-θ)).
Corollary 2.6 (proof): the size of a weighted random dominating set is dominated in convex order by a binomial count with the same mean.

Finite illustration: at p = 1/2, ultra-log-concavity fails for 636 of 32,768 labelled graphs on 6 vertices and 11 of 20,000 sampled graphs on 18 vertices; almost every failure is at the second nonzero count.

Credit and limits: large-mean second-moment bounds are standard (Wieland–Godbole, Glebov–Liebenau–Szabó, Mitsche–Pérez-Giménez–Prałat); Poisson approximation uses Ross, Theorem 4.14. Asymptotic only; p → 1 and p(log n)² → 0 are open.
